strengths: Clear empirical analysis showing complementary strengths of RL (effective on easy questions) and SFT (effective on hard questions), with well-designed motivation experiments (Figure 1)
Strong experimental results: 51.1% overall accuracy, +5.2 points above strongest zero-RL baseline, consistent improvements across six diverse benchmarks (AIME, AMC, MATH500, OlympiadBench, MMLU-Pro)
Significant efficiency gains: uses only 13% of demonstration data compared to SFT while achieving better accuracy and generating ~10x shorter solutions (1,061 vs 10,166 tokens)

Comprehensive experimental validation including ablation studies justifying design choices (all/uniform/random scheduling), training dynamics analysis, and generalization to multiple model sizes (1.5B, 7B)
Well-executed methodology: reproducible with detailed experimental settings, proper baselines, and transparent implementation details (VERL, MATH-VERIFY)
Practical value: simpler and more direct approach compared to complex methods like LUFFY, with adaptive scheduling that requires fewer hyperparameters
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward interleaving of RL and SFT on hard questions (acc(q)=0); incremental over existing combined approaches (LUFFY, Light-R1)

Unfair experimental comparisons: SFT baseline not given adaptive scheduling; cost of obtaining high-quality CoT solutions from stronger models/annotators not analyzed; '13% data' claim somewhat misleading regarding true resource requirements

Underspecified practical details: unclear how high-quality solutions are obtained online, what computational overhead this entails, how sensitive results are to solution quality, exact SFT scheduling (N≥M timing), alignment between training rollout and validation difficulty classification

Limited evaluation scope: all benchmarks math-focused (aligned with training domain); MMLU-Pro shows only modest OOD improvements; no evaluation on code generation or other reasoning domains; results only on Qwen models

Weak theoretical justification: claims about RL's inability to find new solutions lack depth; no analysis of what specific reasoning patterns SFT teaches on hard questions; no qualitative examples of learned improvements
Suboptimal hardest question selection: acc(q)=0 threshold appears arbitrary; Hard category questions (acc∈[0.125,0.25]) might be better for learning; no ablation on this critical hyperparameter

Missing analyses: no qualitative solution examples, no characterization of learnable vs. unlearnable hard questions, limited discussion of failure modes, incomplete understanding of which problem types benefit from this approach

strengths: Insightful empirical analysis of RL vs. SFT training dynamics across question difficulty levels (Section 2.1), providing clear evidence for complementary strengths
Strong empirical results on math benchmarks with +5.2 point improvement over strongest baseline (Oat-Zero) and superior efficiency (~10x shorter responses than SFT)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including multiple benchmarks, ablation studies validating design choices, and extension to multiple model sizes
Well-motivated interleaving strategy that naturally adapts scheduling based on analysis, with effective visualizations and clear presentation
Thorough ablation studies (ReLIFT-all, -uniform, -random) demonstrating importance of both scheduling and question selection strategy
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution is a straightforward scheduling heuristic for combining standard GRPO and SFT without significant algorithmic innovation
Crude definition of 'hardest' questions (acc(q)=0 from 8 samples) lacks justification; no sensitivity analysis; no exploration of alternative thresholds; introduces classification noise

Critical reproducibility gaps: source of high-quality CoT solutions unclear (stronger model vs. human); no specification of which model/version; no cost analysis; unclear whether collection is online or offline
Misleading data efficiency claim: the '13% of SFT data' comparison ignores the cost of obtaining hardest-question solutions; no accounting for R1 computation or annotation labor

Severely limited evaluation scope: all experiments on mathematical reasoning only (MMLU-Pro is still multiple-choice); no evaluation on code, logic, or other domains; generalizability to non-verifiable-reward tasks unknown

Weak theoretical understanding: claims about RL learning 'existing knowledge' vs SFT 'new knowledge' are intuitive but unvalidated; no principled explanation for why interleaving should outperform sequential approaches; motivating experiment uses small scale (8K examples)
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or multiple seeds; small test sets (AIME ~25 questions) could have high variance; single-run results only

Incomplete implementation details: identical learning rates for RL and interleaved SFT despite different typical practices; entropy analysis lacks rigorous validation; unclear why this scheduling emerges vs. explicit design
Overselling of claims: title suggests RL has 'fundamental limitations' but method still requires collecting high-quality solutions externally, not addressing core RL limitations
Missing ablations: no sensitivity to buffer size M, no analysis of different solution sources, no cost-accuracy trade-off curves

strengths: Insightful empirical analysis of RL vs SFT across difficulty levels (Section 2.1) provides clear motivation and intuition
Strong empirical results: 51.1% accuracy (+5.2 over zero-RL baselines, +5.6 over RL, +2.2 over SFT) with only 13% of demonstration data
Comprehensive evaluation across 5 competition-level benchmarks, 1 OOD benchmark, and 3 model sizes demonstrating generality
Rigorous ablation studies (Table 2) validating that both scheduling strategy and hard-example selection are critical
Training dynamics analysis (Figure 3) effectively explains why ReLIFT maintains higher entropy and sustained exploration
Significant practical efficiency gains: ~10x more concise solutions than SFT while achieving higher accuracy
Well-structured presentation with clear motivation and good visualizations
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combining RL and SFT is not new; the core contribution of focusing on hardest questions is incremental relative to LUFFY
Modest improvement over most relevant baseline: only +1.4 points over LUFFY (49.7% → 51.1%), and fair comparison complicated by different training data compositions
Misleading 'online' fine-tuning claims: CoT solutions come from stronger models (R1) or humans, requiring pre-computation rather than true online generation during training
Contradicts data efficiency narrative: while using 13% of SFT data, the method depends on high-quality R1 solutions; sensitivity to solution quality not analyzed
Missing ablations on design choices: no sensitivity analysis for difficulty thresholds (0.75, 0.625, 0.125), buffer threshold M, or how the method behaves when few hardest questions are encountered
Unclear implementation details: how is acc(q) computed during rollouts? What happens when the buffer is empty? Is difficulty classification static or recomputed?
Data contamination concerns: training data overlaps with public benchmarks; with long CoT responses, memorization of reasoning patterns is a potential confound
Baseline reproducibility: zero-RL results reported from prior work rather than independently verified; only LUFFY independently reproduced
Limited failure case analysis: when does ReLIFT underperform? What about boundary-case questions near difficulty transitions?
Scalability questions: as models improve, definition of 'hardest' questions changes; unclear if method scales to much larger models or when acc(q)=0 questions are rare

strengths: Well-motivated empirical analysis showing complementary strengths of RL (easier questions) and SFT (harder questions), with clear visualization of training dynamics across difficulty levels

Strong empirical results with +6.7 point average improvement over prior RLVR methods and state-of-the-art 52.6% accuracy, while using less demonstration data (8K vs 46K) and compute (52×8 vs 57-113.5×8 GPU hours)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including multiple baselines (pure SFT, pure RL, hybrid methods like LUFFY), consistent improvements across model scales (1.5B to 8B parameters), and ablation studies demonstrating importance of scheduling and data selection
Practical method design with online solution collection that reduces reliance on pre-collected datasets and adaptive interleaving that naturally schedules more SFT early when needed most
Good reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, dataset specifications, implementation details, and systematic comparison with properly configured baselines
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is collecting failed examples (acc=0) during RL and fine-tuning with entropy regularization—a straightforward combination rather than a fundamental advance, with prior work exploring RL+SFT combinations (SFT→RL, LUFFY)

Shallow mechanistic analysis of why the method works: shows that RL and SFT are complementary but provides limited insight into underlying causes; entropy regularization choice appears empirically tuned rather than principled

Difficulty classification using base model accuracy with thresholds chosen to ensure balanced splits is somewhat circular; specifically targeting acc(q)=0 trivializes the hardest category definition; no ablation on alternative thresholds (e.g., acc(q)≤0.2)

Practical concerns about solution collection underexplored: requires external DeepSeek-R1 or human expert access during training; no analysis of solution error rates, sensitivity to quality, or actual feasibility/cost at scale

Narrow evaluation scope: almost exclusively mathematical reasoning (5 math benchmarks); code generation mentioned in intro but not evaluated; MMLU-Pro shows modest OOD gains (53.9% vs 52.6% LUFFY); generalization to other reasoning domains unknown

Experimental design fairness issues: different demonstration amounts across comparisons (46K for SFT baselines, 8K-8.6K for others); no confidence intervals or statistical significance testing despite small AIME test sets; different learning rates not fully justified

Response length tradeoff not thoroughly analyzed: ReLIFT shorter than SFT but longer than RL; unclear if conciseness is beneficial or represents missed learning opportunities, particularly for hard questions where longer reasoning may be valuable

Missing ablations on key design choices: no exploration of buffer size sensitivity, alternative scheduling patterns beyond uniform-8 steps, or threshold variation for hardness criterion (why exactly acc=0?)

Limited statistical rigor: no error bars or confidence intervals reported; small evaluation sets (especially AIME) warrant multiple runs or significance tests; robustness across data/initialization unclear

strengths: Clear empirical motivation with insightful analysis of RL vs SFT performance across question difficulties (Figure 1)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 math benchmarks plus OOD benchmark, with multiple hybrid baselines (RL w/ SFT loss, SFT then RL, LUFFY)
Resource-efficient approach achieving best results (52.6%) while using fewer GPU hours (52×8) and demonstrations (8K) than competing methods
Consistent improvements across diverse base models (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, 7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) demonstrating practical applicability
Rigorous ablation studies (Figure 4) clearly demonstrating importance of both adaptive scheduling and hard example selection
Useful analysis of training dynamics showing ReLIFT maintains higher entropy and exploration compared to pure RL
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution (interleaving RL with fine-tuning on hard examples) is relatively straightforward and incremental over prior work like LUFFY and SFT→RL approaches; entropy regularization is standard practice

Demonstration data sourcing inadequately specified: paper states solutions come from 'pre-collection or consulting stronger models/humans' but never clarifies actual implementation; if DeepSeek-R1 was used, this contradicts efficiency claims

Narrow evaluation scope limited to math reasoning (5/6 benchmarks); MMLU-Pro is not truly out-of-distribution given math-only training; generalization to code, reasoning tasks, or other domains completely undemonstrated

Circular evaluation logic: identifying 'hardest questions' as acc(q)=0 on current model means SFT obviously helps; real question of whether interleaving is optimal compared to other orderings is not deeply explored

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: paper shows empirically that interleaving works but lacks theoretical depth explaining why; unclear whether benefits derive from preventing entropy collapse, maintaining exploration, preventing distribution shift, or other factors

Baseline comparison concerns: previous RLVR results (SimpleRL-Zero, OpenReasoner-Zero, etc.) taken from LUFFY paper rather than independently reproduced; pure RL baseline (46.9%) appears weak; SFT→RL v2 uses different demonstration splitting strategy
Overstated claims: paper claims 'significantly more concise solutions' but ReLIFT (3502 tokens) is actually longer than pure RL (2175 tokens), only shorter than SFT (5533 tokens)
Lack of statistical rigor: no significance testing or confidence intervals provided for claimed improvements (e.g., 52.6% vs LUFFY's 50.9%); no error bars across multiple runs

Incomplete ablations: entropy hyperparameter α tested only over narrow range (0 to 1e-3); sensitivity to difficulty thresholds (0/8, 1-2/8, 3-5/8, 6-8/8) not explored; number of SFT steps per RL phase not varied
Reproducibility concerns: code availability not mentioned; demonstration data collection process not fully specified; filtering of incorrect model-generated CoTs not quantified

strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical analysis of RL vs. SFT across question difficulty levels (Section 2.1, Figure 1), providing strong motivation for the proposed interleaving strategy
Impressive empirical results: +6.7 point improvement over previous RLVR methods while using 5.75x fewer demonstrations (8K vs. 46K) and 30% fewer GPU hours
Consistent improvements across three model sizes/architectures (Qwen 1.5B, 7B; LLaMA 8B), demonstrating generalizability within the model family
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with fair comparisons to strong baselines (pure RL, pure SFT, RL w/ SFT loss, SFT then RL, LUFFY) across six diverse benchmarks
Thorough ablation studies proving importance of both scheduling strategy and hard example selection (Figure 4), with clear evidence that simple alternatives fail
Training dynamics analysis (Figure 3) and behavioral analysis (Figure 8) providing insights into why ReLIFT works better at maintaining exploration and planning
Practical simplicity of the method—straightforward to implement with no complex architectural changes
Clear presentation with well-designed figures and detailed experimental setup in appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: combining RL and SFT is not new (LUFFY exists); the contribution is primarily the specific interleaving strategy, which is more engineering-focused than conceptual

Arbitrary definition of 'hardest' questions as acc(q)=0 (0/8 correct): excludes potentially important intermediate difficulty questions with 0 < acc(q) ≤ 0.125; no justification or exploration of alternative thresholds

Critical practical limitation: method requires high-quality external CoT solutions from DeepSeek-R1 or human experts, undermining reproducibility and true 'online' applicability; the claimed advantage of reducing demonstration data is negated by needing external annotations
No sensitivity analysis on solution quality: unclear how results degrade with lower-quality external models (e.g., GPT-4 vs. DeepSeek-R1), making real-world applicability uncertain

Limited generalization beyond mathematical reasoning: all main experiments on math with verifiable rewards; only one OOD benchmark (MMLU-Pro) with modest gains; unclear if method applies to other reasoning domains, tasks without verifiable rewards, or different languages

Design choices appear ad-hoc: entropy regularization coefficient α=1×10⁻⁴ selected via grid search without principled justification; threshold M and adaptive scheduling heuristics lack theoretical grounding
Scalability questions inadequately addressed: all experiments on small models (1.5B-8B); unclear how approach scales to 70B+ models where generating external solutions becomes prohibitively expensive
Missing ablations and analyses: no exploration of alternative difficulty thresholds, effect of M (batch size), comparison to curriculum learning approaches, or principled scheduling strategies

Some comparison fairness concerns: SFT then RL (v1) uses different dataset sizes; baselines from other papers limit direct comparisons; improvements of ReLIFT(v2) over SFT then RL(v2) are modest (1.7 points)

Ambiguous response length analysis: unclear whether longer responses consistently improve reasoning quality or reflect verbosity; the interpretation of stable length for Hardest questions in RL could be debated
